definition.text: Return on investment is the ratio of the profit an investment earns to what it cost.

facts.text: A high return on investment means the gains compare well with the cost.
It is used to judge how efficient one investment is or to compare several, and the one with the highest return is usually chosen first.
A simple form is the gain from the investment minus its cost, divided by its cost.
Example: $10,000 invested plus $200 in fees, worth $12,500 after a year with $300 in dividends, gives an annual return.
It is not adjusted for time, so long-term investments need a discounted version using net present value.
Traditional ROI ignores the value and risks of natural and social capital because it leaves out environmental, social and governance performance.

definition.text: Return on integration widens return on investment to count the long-term environmental and social returns of an investment alongside financial ones.

facts.text: The social cost of carbon can be built in to capture the damage an investment's emissions do to society.
It supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, combining financial, environmental and social results in one balance sheet.
A related method, social return on investment, measures environmental and social value not shown in ordinary accounts.

definition.text: A fiduciary is a person trusted to look after money or other assets for someone else and to act only in that person's interest.

facts.text: Trustees, financial advisers and managers of pension funds and endowments are fiduciaries.
Under Delaware law, which governs most large US firms, directors owe duties of care, loyalty and good faith.
A fiduciary must not let personal interest conflict with duty, nor profit from the position without informed consent.

title: Fiduciary duty and ESG

definition.text: A debate over whether investors' legal duty to beneficiaries allows, or even requires, them to weigh environmental, social and governance issues.

facts.text: A 2015 report, 'Fiduciary Duty in the 21st Century', concluded that ignoring long-term value drivers including ESG is itself a failure of fiduciary duty.
In the United States, some question whether pension funds that weigh such factors break their duty to maximise returns.
A 2005 legal report for UNEP similarly found that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably required.
One US state pension board blocked fossil fuel divestment on fiduciary grounds, though a 2019 analysis found the divested fund would have earned more.

contested_note: Investors and lawyers dispute whether fiduciary duty is a barrier to considering ESG issues.
